title: Treasury Yields Hit Multi-Decade Highs as US National Debt Approaches $40 Trillion
excerpt: The 30-year bond yield reached a 25-year peak of 5.216% while the 10-year hit its highest since 2007, reflecting investor unease over structurally large deficits.
body:
• The 30-year Treasury bond yield hit 5.216% at auction — the highest in 25 years — while the 10-year note cleared at 4.683%, the highest since 2007.
  • U.S. national debt is approaching $40 trillion, with the Congressional Budget Office projecting a roughly $2.1 trillion budget deficit this fiscal year.
  • Despite elevated yields, investor demand has held up, with analysts seeing no signs of a buyer's strike or active selling by bond vigilantes.

U.S. Treasury yields have surged to levels not seen in decades, driven by a potent combination of swelling national debt, wide fiscal deficits, and investor anxiety about Washington's ability to manage its borrowing costs.

Two auctions in the past week sent unmistakable signals. The 10-year note sale cleared at a high yield of 4.683%, the highest in 19 years, while the 30-year bond auction stopped at 5.216% — a 25-year peak not seen since 2001, when a similar sale commanded a 5.52% yield, according to Reuters and The Times of London.

A Structural Repricing

The yield climb is not the product of a single shock. Long-term Treasury yields have risen steadily this year as investors grapple with heavy government borrowing, resilient economic growth, sticky inflation, and rising geopolitical costs — including an estimated $37.5 billion already spent on the Iran conflict, with the Trump administration requesting a supplemental $67 billion.

"The overall market environment is definitely requiring Treasury to pay more to borrow."

— Zachary Griffiths, Head of Macro Strategy, CreditSights

U.S. national debt is approaching a record $40 trillion, according to the Treasury Department. The Congressional Budget Office projects a roughly $2.1 trillion budget deficit this fiscal year, with deficits running at 5% to 6% of GDP — roughly double the 3% level many economists consider sustainable. Debt-to-GDP has already topped 100% and is projected to exceed its post-World War II peak of 106% by 2036.

"It is more of a problem longer run if we're going to run budget deficits of 5% to 6% of GDP," Griffiths told Reuters. "Part of that is a fiscal and inflation risk premium, among other things."

No Buyer's Strike — Yet

Despite the eye-catching yields, demand for Treasuries has held up. The same forces driving yields higher are also boosting the compensation investors receive for holding U.S. government debt, making a 5.3% nominal return on a 30-year risk-free asset compelling for pension funds, insurers, and asset managers with long-term liabilities.

"The appetite for Treasuries is still there and it's just a matter of — at what yield," said Jim Barnes, director of fixed income at Bryn Mawr Trust. "The 10-year at close to 5% and the 30-year at multi-decade highs will attract more buyers for risk-free Treasuries."

Analysts noted no signs of so-called bond vigilantes actively selling Treasuries or of foreign investors broadly retreating. Last week's auction metrics showed no abrupt pullback in overseas demand. U.S. yields remain substantially above those in Japan and other developed markets, creating continued incentive for foreign holders.

Rising Term Premium

A key driver of the yield increase is the growing term premium — the extra compensation investors demand to hold longer-dated debt rather than rolling over shorter-term bonds. This premium has risen as markets price in structurally large deficits and uncertainty about the government's borrowing trajectory.

"We've seen a few trends that are worrying us," said Laureline Renaud-Chatelain, fixed income strategy lead at Pictet Wealth Management, citing the increase in term premium driven partly by high fiscal deficits. She noted this dynamic is pushing the Treasury to skew issuance toward shorter-duration debt, which money market funds have absorbed quickly.

The recent 30-year bond auction drew particular attention because long-dated Treasuries are especially sensitive to concerns about future inflation, fiscal sustainability, and debt supply. Frances Cheung, head of FX and rates strategy at OCBC Bank, said the auction outcome reflects "investor caution against long duration."

What's Next

The higher yields carry real-world consequences. The 10-year Treasury yield serves as a benchmark for pricing 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, which were last pegged at 6.55% — a threshold that can freeze refinancing activity. For the federal government itself, persistently higher borrowing costs mean interest payments will consume an ever-larger share of the budget, potentially crowding out other spending priorities.

"Investors demand more to compensate for sticky inflation and large fiscal deficits," said Ben Bennett, head of investment strategy for Asia at L&G Asset Management. The market, for now, remains well functioning — but it has clearly repriced the cost of financing the world's largest economy.
